case.text:
The low-temperature bonding work began in the current year, so no prior-year status applies. The company undertook a systematic investigation to determine whether structural adhesive bonds on aluminium cured at 60°C could retain lap shear strength through thermal cycling between -30°C and +40°C. Suppliers and published literature offered no cycling data, so the plan began by curing and cycling three commercial low-temperature adhesive systems to establish a baseline. The company then designed a full factorial matrix of two adhesive chemistries, three surface treatments on the aluminium skins and two cure schedules [GAP: names of the chemistries, surface treatments and cure schedules in the matrix]. Each combination used 12 lap shear coupons, with six tested fresh and six after 200 thermal cycles [GAP: lap shear test standard, thermal cycle profile and dwell times]. Comparing strength retention and failure location across combinations addressed the open question from Line 242 of which variable governs retention.

It was hypothesized that if the surface treatment and cure schedule were controlled alongside adhesive chemistry, then bonds cured at 60°C would retain lap shear strength after 200 cycles between -30°C and +40°C at or above the truck body specification [GAP: specification threshold], failing within the adhesive rather than at the interface. The hypothesis would be disproved if every combination lost strength comparable to the roughly 40% loss seen in commercial systems, or continued to fail at the interface or primer. The test criterion was cycled strength as a percentage of fresh strength for the same combination. After primer-layer failure appeared, the company narrowed the hypothesis. A 2-hour hold at 40°C before ramping to 60°C, combined with a silane primer, would let the primer finish reacting before the adhesive gelled, removing primer-layer failure while meeting the specification after cycling.

The first experiment asked whether off-the-shelf low-temperature adhesives could survive thermal cycling. The company cured three commercial low-temperature systems at low cure temperature and cycled them between -30°C and +40°C [GAP: product names and per-system results]. All three cured, yet lap shear strength after cycling dropped by about 40%, showing that successful low-temperature cure did not predict durability under cycling. No supplier or literature data could explain the loss, so the company stopped screening products and moved to the factorial matrix to isolate individual variables. This established that commercial low-temperature adhesives alone could not meet the requirement and that cycling behaviour had to be characterized directly.

The second experiment set out to identify which variable controlled strength retention after cycling. The company expected adhesive chemistry to dominate and tested all twelve combinations of chemistry, surface treatment and cure schedule. Instead, surface treatment had the larger effect: the plain abraded surface lost the most strength, while a silane primer kept about 85% [GAP: results for the second cure schedule and any interaction effects]. Fresh strength with the silane primer was acceptable, but cycled coupons still failed at the primer layer rather than in the adhesive [GAP: failure mode analysis method]. The company therefore shifted its focus from the adhesive to the timing of primer reaction relative to adhesive gelation. This showed that interface chemistry, not the adhesive itself, was the main factor in strength retention after cycling.

The third experiment addressed whether primer-layer failure could be removed at low cure temperature. The primed coupons in the matrix had used cure schedules that went directly to 60°C. From the failure location, the team reasoned that the adhesive gelled before the silane primer had finished reacting. This interpretation rested on failure location, not on a direct measurement of reaction state. The company revised the schedule to a stepped cure: a 2-hour hold at 40°C, then a ramp to 60°C [GAP: how the 40°C and 2-hour values were chosen and whether alternatives were tried]. Extending the low-temperature stage risked reducing overall bond performance, yet primed flat coupons kept 91% of lap shear strength after 200 cycles and met the truck body specification. The company concluded that the sequence of primer reaction and adhesive gelation controls the cycling durability of these bonds. It remains open whether the sequence holds at the thicker bond line found in curved panel corners.
case.storylineText: Meridian Materials makes bonded composite panels for refrigerated truck bodies. The project aimed to cure the structural adhesive at 60 degrees instead of the normal 120 degrees, so that panels with foam cores and wiring already inside could be bonded without the foam deforming or the wiring insulation softening. The technological uncertainty was whether any adhesive chemistry could keep its lap shear strength through thermal cycling between -30 and +40 degrees when cured at 60 degrees. Three commercial low-temperature systems cured but lost about forty percent of lap shear strength after cycling. Suppliers had no data for cycling at those extremes, and the published literature covered only steady temperatures. The team ran a test matrix of two adhesive chemistries, three surface treatments on the aluminium skins and two cure schedules. Each combination used twelve lap shear coupons, half tested fresh and half after 200 thermal cycles. The first round showed that surface treatment mattered more than adhesive chemistry. The plain abraded surface lost the most strength, while a silane primer kept about eighty-five percent. The cycled primed coupons still failed at the primer layer rather than in the adhesive. From this the team reasoned that the primer needed to finish reacting before the adhesive gelled, and tested a stepped cure: a two-hour hold at 40 degrees before going to 60 degrees. The stepped cure kept ninety-one percent of strength after cycling, which met the truck body specification. The advancement is knowledge of how primer reaction and cure staging control the failure mode of low-temperature-cured bonds under thermal cycling. That knowledge was established on flat coupons only. It is still unknown whether the stepped cure behaves the same at the thicker bond lines found in curved panel corners, where the bond line is three times thicker. The evidence does not describe what records were kept beyond the coupon test counts and results.
